gi5_begin.topic: Begin in power 1977-1982: Judea and Samaria, the autonomy plan, Golan Law

claims.text: Begin, reported in the Detroit Jewish News of 27 May 1977 (after the 17 May election), said Judaea and Samaria 'cannot be given up in any part', that Arab residents 'can have complete cultural autonomy', and 'It is not an occupied country'.

Shortly after his election win Begin visited the Elon Moreh group at the Kadum military base and told the settlers, 'Soon, there will be many Elon Morehs'; Begin's government served June 1977–August 1981 (first term).

Begin's message to Carter transmitted 9 January 1978: the cabinet had decided to strengthen existing settlements in Pithat Rafiah and 'to establish four additional settlements, all of them in military camps'; he relayed Dayan's account that Carter spoke of 'the illegality of the settlements and their being an obstacle to peace' and Dayan's reply that 'there cannot be a government in Israel that will not establish settlements'.

Israel's Self-Rule Plan of 28 December 1977 (26 points): residents of Judea, Samaria and Gaza to have administrative autonomy; security and public order 'will be the responsibility of the Israeli authorities' (pt 11); free choice of Israeli or Jordanian citizenship (pt 14); 'Residents of Israel will be entitled to acquire land and settle in the areas of Judea, Samaria and the Gaza district' (pt 20); Israel maintains its claim of sovereignty but, knowing other claims exist, proposes 'the question of sovereignty in these areas be left open' (pt 24); review after five years (pt 26).

Golan Heights Law, 14 December 1981, passed 63–21: 'The Law, jurisdiction and administration of the State will take effect in the Golan Heights'; the law does not use the word annexation; Begin presented it to a special cabinet session; UNSC Resolution 497 (17 December 1981), adopted unanimously, declared it null and void and without international legal effect; Reagan said it 'increased the difficulty of seeking peace'; the US suspended the strategic cooperation agreement; the US recognised Israeli sovereignty on 25 March 2019.

gi5_likud.topic: Likud's platform and party bodies on the land, 1977–2017, and the counter-record within Likud

claims.text: The 1977 Likud platform, section 'The Right of the Jewish People to the Land of Israel': 'The right of the Jewish people to the land of Israel is eternal and indisputable'; 'Judea and Samaria will not be handed to any foreign administration'; 'between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty'; a plan relinquishing parts of western Eretz Israel 'undermines our right to the country' and 'unavoidably leads to the establishment of a Palestinian State'.

1977 Likud platform on settlement: settlement 'in all parts of the Land of Israel is the focal point of the Zionist effort to redeem the country'; the government will call on the young to settle, 'while taking care not to dispossess anyone'; on peace: direct negotiations 'without pre-conditions on either side', attendance at Geneva; the platform does not mention Jerusalem.

Likud Central Committee, 12 May 2002 (AP): by show of hands adopted a Netanyahu-backed resolution, 'No Palestinian state will be created west of the Jordan'; Sharon's alternative lost a secret ballot 59–41 per cent; Sharon had called a Palestinian state 'inevitable' and said he would keep leading 'according to the same ideas'; Erekat called the vote 'a real slap in the face' for Bush.

Likud Central Committee, 31 December 2017, unanimously called on the party's elected leaders 'to extend Israeli law and sovereignty in all the areas of liberated settlement in Judea and Samaria' with unhindered construction; not binding on MKs; Netanyahu did not attend and had long opposed such declarations by party bodies; Edelstein, Barkat and ministers backed it; Sa'ar said annexation could come 'in just a few years'.

Netanyahu at Bar-Ilan, 14 June 2009: the West Bank is 'the land of our forefathers', yet Israel would accept 'a demilitarised Palestinian state' alongside the Jewish state on conditions; 'we have no intention of building new settlements or of expropriating additional land for existing settlements'; Jerusalem 'must remain the united capital of Israel'.

gi5_nationstate.topic: Nation-State Law 2018 clause 7 and the 37th government's guidelines and coalition agreement, 2022

claims.text: Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People passed 62–55 with two abstentions early on 19 July 2018. Clause 1: the Land of Israel is 'the historical homeland of the Jewish people'; 'The right to exercise national self-determination in the State of Israel is unique to the Jewish people'. Clause 3: 'Jerusalem, complete and united, is the capital of Israel'. Clause 4: Hebrew the state language; Arabic 'a special status'. Clause 7: 'The state views the development of Jewish settlement as a national value' and will encourage and promote its establishment and consolidation.

Netanyahu called the law's passage a 'defining moment in the annals of Zionism and the history of the state of Israel'; Arab MKs tore up copies, calling it the 'death of democracy'; one called it an 'apartheid' law.

Adalah (Nov 2018): clause 7 read with clause 1, which names the Land of Israel as the homeland, gives constitutional backing to settlement in the West Bank and East Jerusalem and could support Jewish-only towns in the Galilee and Naqab; the law contains no guarantee of equality and defines no borders.

HCJ 5555/18 Hassoun v. The Knesset, 8 July 2021: an 11-justice panel upheld the law 10–1, Justice George Karra dissenting; the majority held the settlement clause is not meant to legalise discrimination or exclusion of non-Jews from state lands, as the State also clarified; equality remains a fundamental principle though most justices said it would have been better to include it; Karra held the clause aims to negate the Qa'adan ruling on equal land allocation; Justice Minister Sa'ar welcomed the ruling.

The 37th government's guidelines, published 28 December 2022: 'The Jewish people has an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel'; 'The government will promote and develop the settlement of all parts of the Land of Israel – in the Galilee, the Negev, the Golan Heights and Judea and Samaria'; also to 'preserve the Jewish character of the state' and respect the practices of all religions.

The Likud–Religious Zionism coalition agreement (signed 1 December 2022) states, as reported, that 'the prime minister will lead the formulation and advancement of policies within the framework of applying sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, while choosing the timing and weighing all of the State of Israel's national and international interests'.

The 1 December 2022 deal gave Religious Zionism a ministerial post in the Defense Ministry responsible for the Civil Administration and the District Coordination and Liaison offices, acting 'with the coordination and agreement of the prime minister', plus the WZO Settlement Division; Smotrich said the government would 'regulate and develop the settlement enterprise'; Gallant signed the transfer of West Bank powers on 23 February 2023.
